metadata.name: AI Database Rule Framework
metadata.description: Complete rule library extracted from 23 production MySQL databases across 9 business domains. Use for AI schema generation, RAG retrieval, and validation.

usage.RAG_retrieval: Embed each rule as a vector chunk. Retrieve by trigger_when keywords.
usage.prompt_injection: Inject matched rules into system prompt before schema generation.
usage.validation: After generation, check output against enforce/avoid lists per activated rule.
usage.fine_tuning: Use rule_id lists as expected_rules field in training data.

enforce: _header_all suffix for master entity tables
_details_all suffix for child or secondary record tables
_transaction_all suffix for event or ledger record tables
_configuration_all suffix for temporal configuration tables
_archive_all suffix for historical mirror tables
_life_cycle_all suffix for status change audit tables
avoid: random table suffixes
mixed naming patterns in same schema
domain-specific random suffixes
rules.reason: Keeps schema predictable and AI-generatable. Anyone reading table names instantly knows its role.

trigger_when: any table that has a UI-visible identifier
enforce: every table must have an integer auto-increment primary key column named 'id'
every business entity must have a human-readable business ID (varchar, prefixed)
business IDs must be generated from unique_id_header_all registry table
business IDs must use alphabetic prefix (e.g. EMP-, INV-, ORD-)
avoid: using auto-increment integer IDs in UI or user-facing communications
manual business ID generation outside central registry
exposing raw database PKs to end users
rules.reason: Decouples internal DB identity from business identity. Allows renumbering and prefix changes without schema migration.

trigger_when: updating records that have business significance
any table where data can change after creation
enforce: Layer 1 - status field: soft delete/deactivate rather than hard delete
Layer 2 - old_* inline columns: store previous value before overwriting (e.g. old_mobile_no, old_salary)
Layer 3 - _archive_all table: full row snapshot copied to archive table on every significant change
avoid: hard DELETE statements on business-critical data
overwriting columns without preserving old value
relying on application logs as the only history
rules.reason: Production systems need audit trails for compliance, dispute resolution, and debugging. Three layers cover different granularities.

trigger_when: status-driven entities with more than 2 states
entities where the history of state changes matters
enforce: create dedicated _life_cycle_all table for complex entities
store exact datetime for each status transition
store previous_status and new_status on each life cycle row
store who triggered the transition (employee_id or user_id)
avoid: single status column with no transition history
relying on modified_on timestamp to infer state history
rules.reason: Compliance and dispute resolution require knowing not just current state but every state change and when it happened.

trigger_when: two entity types have different event structures
different business logic applies per type
different lifecycle or approval chains per type
enforce: create separate tables for fundamentally different business structures
do not force different domain entities into one table with a type column
avoid: single giant table with nullable columns for unrelated workflows
type-discriminated single table when structures diverge significantly
rules.reason: Mixing domains in one table causes sparse nulls, confusing queries, and makes AI generation ambiguous.

trigger_when: any price that can change over time
enforce: applied_from date/datetime column on every rate record
valid_till or applicable_to date/datetime column
operational_status column to mark past / current / upcoming
never overwrite a rate row — insert a new row with new dates
avoid: single rate column that gets updated in place
no history of what rate applied when
rules.reason: Any financial dispute requires knowing which rate was active at the time of a transaction.

trigger_when: any financial transaction in Indian market
enforce: separate sgst_amount column (State GST)
separate cgst_amount column (Central GST)
store both as DECIMAL, not computed-only
store percentage values separately: sgst_percentage, cgst_percentage
avoid: single combined tax_amount column
computing tax only at display time without storing breakdown
rules.reason: Indian GST law requires SGST and CGST to be reported separately on every invoice. Merged tax columns are non-compliant.

enforce: status fields must be integer type (tinyint or int)
every possible value must be documented inline in SQL COMMENT
comment format: '1=active, 2=inactive, 3=suspended, 4=deleted'
avoid: varchar status fields
undocumented integer status values
boolean for status with more than 2 possible states
rules.reason: Integer status fields are indexed efficiently. Inline COMMENTs make the schema self-documenting without needing external docs.

trigger_when: any new business ID type is needed
any table that requires a human-readable unique identifier
enforce: all business IDs generated from a single unique_id_header_all table
unique_id_header_all has one row per entity type with prefix + last_id + current_id
ID format: PREFIX-NNNNN (e.g. EMP-00001)
never generate IDs independently in application code
avoid: random UUID as default business ID
multiple independent ID generators for same entity type
application-side ID generation without DB coordination
rules.reason: Centralised registry prevents duplicate business IDs across concurrent transactions and ensures sequential auditability.

enforce: table_inside_table_all tracks row count limits per table
first_alert_on threshold column triggers notification
maximum_row_limit column triggers stop flag
is_stopable flag prevents further inserts when limit hit
avoid: relying solely on external monitoring tools for DB capacity
no capacity awareness in schema design
rules.reason: DB self-monitors without needing external APM tools. Critical for shared hosting or limited-resource environments.

trigger_when: transaction requiring sign-off from multiple people
enforce: store approval_1 through approval_N inline on the transaction row itself
each approval_N column stores: approver_id + status + datetime as encoded string
fixed maximum approver count known at design time
approval status lives on same transaction row — no separate approval table for simple workflows
avoid: normalised approval step tables for simple linear workflows
dynamic approval chain tables when chain depth is fixed
rules.reason: For fixed-depth approval chains, inline columns eliminate JOINs and make the approval state readable in one row.

trigger_when: any process where step B cannot happen without step A
enforce: use NOT NULL constraints to force required fields before progression
use CHECK constraints to enforce valid state combinations
document every constraint rule in column COMMENT
business rules encoded in schema, not only in application
avoid: business workflow logic only in frontend or application layer
no DB-level enforcement of workflow rules
rules.reason: Application code can be bypassed. Schema constraints cannot. Critical workflow gates must be enforced at DB level.

enforce: form configuration table defines field name, type, compulsory flag, default value
field visibility controlled by DB rows, not hardcoded in frontend
field validation rules stored in DB columns
UI renders dynamically from DB config — changing form = data update not code deploy
rules.reason: Eliminates code deployments for UI changes. Clients can self-configure forms without developer involvement.

trigger_when: two related entity types share more than 80% column structure
same lifecycle applies to both types
entity type is a simple binary distinction
enforce: single table with type_flag column when structure overlap exceeds 80%
document type values in COMMENT: '1=employee, 2=guard'
avoid: separate tables when structure is nearly identical and lifecycle is identical
duplicate maintenance of two identical schemas
rules.reason: When two entity types are structurally near-identical, splitting wastes schema real estate and duplicates maintenance.

enforce: store only file URL or path in DB — never binary file content
file_type or mime_type column always alongside the URL
uploaded_by tracking column
uploaded_on datetime column
cloud_path or storage_path column for bucket reference
avoid: storing binary BLOB data in primary entity tables
URL without accompanying type metadata
rules.reason: Binary files in DB bloat storage and slow backups. URLs with type metadata are portable and cloud-storage ready.

enforce: hierarchical location tables: country → state → district → city → area
parent_child relationships with FK between levels
geo_code or pin_code on each level
latitude and longitude on city/area level
rules.reason: Geo hierarchies drive reporting aggregation and permission scoping. Flat address strings cannot be aggregated or filtered by region.

trigger_when: deciding how to encode a status or state column
any column with a fixed set of possible values
enforce: int + COMMENT when many states exist (5+) or ordering/comparison matters
abbreviated string + COMMENT when 2-5 states and human readability matters more
ENUM for 2-5 truly immutable value sets that will never expand
choose encoding deliberately based on cardinality and expansion likelihood
avoid: arbitrary choice of encoding type
ENUM when values may expand in future
rules.reason: ENUM is cheap but painful to alter. Int is flexible but unreadable. String is readable but unindexed. Pick deliberately.

enforce: created_by column: user_id or employee_id who created the record
updated_by column: user_id or employee_id who last modified
created_on datetime column
modified_on datetime column
ip_address logging for sensitive operations
rules.reason: Audit columns answer: who did what and when. Essential for compliance, dispute resolution, and debugging.

enforce: configuration_all tables with effective dates
active flag column
version tracking via line_no
never hardcode configuration values in application code
rules.reason: Dynamic configuration eliminates code deployments for business rule changes. Ops team controls behaviour via data.

trigger_when: any business-critical entity that can be deactivated or removed
records that may need to be restored
enforce: status-based soft deletion: set status = inactive/deleted, never DELETE row
deleted_on datetime column: timestamp of deletion
deleted_by column: who performed the deletion
avoid: hard DELETE queries on business entities
no way to recover deleted records
rules.reason: Hard deletes are irreversible. Soft deletes allow restoration, audit, and cross-reference integrity.

trigger_when: settings that can change over time
config or rate tables with history
enforce: line_no=0 for master/summary row
line_no 1, 2, 3... for successive versions or detail rows
MAX(line_no) within a group = current active version
older line_no rows become historical record
rules.reason: Enables in-table versioning without separate history tables for moderate-change-frequency entities.

trigger_when: entities share column structure but belong to different domains
same columns but different lifecycle, ownership, or business meaning
enforce: create separate tables per domain even when column list is nearly identical
domain ownership takes priority over DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle
rules.reason: Different domains diverge over time. Sharing tables forces coupling that becomes painful at schema revision time.

trigger_when: data is always queried and updated as a complete unit
normalising would create a JOIN-heavy read with no benefit
enforce: flatten fixed-depth hierarchy inline when always retrieved together
shift1_name, shift1_start, shift1_end, shift2_name, shift2_start... pattern is valid
avoid: normalising into child rows when entity is always read/written as one unit
rules.reason: Normalisation has a JOIN cost. When the full structure is always needed, denormalisation is the correct engineering choice.

trigger_when: any entity with a running financial balance
enforce: closing_balance column on every transaction row — updated at write time
current_wallet_bal column on the entity (wallet owner) row
full transaction history table alongside the balance columns
avoid: computing balance with SUM() at read time for operational queries
no balance column — balance only derivable via aggregation
rules.reason: SUM() on large transaction tables is slow and inconsistent under concurrent writes. Stored balance is O(1) read.

trigger_when: any column storing a monetary amount
any column storing a price, fee, charge, tax, or discount
enforce: use DECIMAL(10,2) for amounts up to 99,999,999.99
use DECIMAL(12,2) for large amounts (property prices, enterprise billing)
never use float or double for monetary values
avoid: float for money — IEEE 754 floating point has rounding errors
double for money — same rounding issue as float
rules.reason: Float/double rounding errors accumulate in financial calculations. A 0.001 error per transaction becomes thousands in aggregate.

trigger_when: any table needing creation or modification tracking
enforce: creation timestamp column must be named: created_on (datetime)
modification timestamp column must be named: modified_on (datetime)
apply consistently across ALL tables in the schema
avoid: created_at / updated_at (Laravel convention — only in framework tables)
insert_date, last_modified, timestamp — inconsistent naming
rules.reason: Consistent timestamp naming allows universal tooling and queries across all tables without inspecting each schema.

enforce: all FK constraints must have explicit names using fk_ prefix
naming pattern: fk_childtable_parenttable or fk_column
avoid: anonymous constraint names — database assigns random names making migration painful
rules.reason: Named FKs make migration scripts, error messages, and schema documentation readable and refactorable.

enforce: all indexes must have explicit names using idx_ prefix
naming pattern: idx_tablename_columns (e.g. idx_employee_agency_id)
avoid: anonymous index names
relying on ORM to auto-name indexes
rules.reason: Named indexes make EXPLAIN output readable and index management scriptable.

trigger_when: tables queried by multiple columns simultaneously
enforce: composite indexes built on actual production query WHERE clause patterns
column order in composite index matches query filter priority (most selective first)
validate index design with EXPLAIN before finalising
rules.reason: Wrong column order in composite index makes it useless. Index design must be driven by real query patterns.

trigger_when: emergency kill switches for the application
enforce: factory_reset_all table with exactly one data row
each feature flag is a typed column (web_status, reg_status, login_status)
column values: 1=on, 0=off with COMMENT documentation
rules.reason: Single-row configuration table allows instant platform-wide feature toggling without code deployment.

enforce: otp_attempt_count column: counts wrong OTP entries
otp_sent_count column: counts how many OTPs were resent
blocked_till datetime column: automatic unblock when timestamp passes
expires_at datetime column: OTP expiry separate from block expiry
avoid: is_blocked boolean flag — requires manual unblock
relying only on application-layer rate limiting
rules.reason: DB-level rate limiting persists across server restarts and cannot be bypassed by direct API calls.

rules.rule_name: Prefixed Column Naming for JOIN-Heavy Schemas
trigger_when: schemas with many JOINs across tables
tables that share common column names (id, name, status, mobile_no)
complex reporting queries spanning multiple tables
enforce: prefix all columns with abbreviated table identifier (emp_id, bha_name, pld_status)
eliminates column name collisions in multi-table JOINs without aliasing
rules.reason: Prefixed columns make JOINs self-documenting and eliminate ambiguous column name errors in complex queries.

trigger_when: tables expected to exceed 2 billion rows
enforce: use bigint for PKs on tables with projected row count > 2 billion
use int for entity/master tables (employees, products, agencies)
rules.reason: int PK maxes at ~2.1 billion. IoT and high-frequency tables can hit this in 1-2 years. bigint adds no meaningful overhead.

trigger_when: any count displayed in real-time UI
enforce: maintain count columns on parent entity row (no_of_guards, pending_count, active_branch)
increment/decrement counter at write time when child records change
count column is always consistent — never stale
avoid: SELECT COUNT(*) at read time for operational counts displayed in UI
computing aggregates on large child tables during user-facing requests
rules.reason: COUNT() on millions of rows is slow. Stored counters are O(1). The slight write overhead is always worth the read performance gain.

trigger_when: entities that have both a current state and a history of events
any entity where both snapshot and timeline matter
enforce: _header_all table stores current state snapshot (always fresh, one row per entity)
_transaction_all table stores all events chronologically (append-only)
rules.reason: Snapshot enables O(1) current state reads. Event log enables full audit and timeline reconstruction. Both are needed.

trigger_when: workflows that can be interrupted and resumed
enforce: last_transaction_id or last_ple_id column on session row
points to the last completed transaction in the session
enables instant recovery to last known state without full table scan
rules.reason: Network drops, app crashes, and browser closes happen. Resume pointers allow seamless continuation without data loss.

trigger_when: content that must display in multiple languages
enforce: separate column per language: que_description_eng, que_description_hindi
use this pattern for fixed, small language sets only
avoid: separate language translation table for fixed 2-language systems — JOIN overhead not justified
rules.reason: For fixed 2-3 language systems, inline columns are simpler, faster, and easier to manage than translation tables.

trigger_when: any entity that can be deactivated or suspended
entities where knowing when they were deactivated matters
enforce: dedicated deactivated_on datetime column alongside status field
NULL until entity is deactivated, then set once and never changed
avoid: relying on modified_on to determine deactivation time (modified_on changes for other reasons too)
rules.reason: status=inactive tells you the current state. deactivated_on tells you exactly when. Both are needed for SLA and compliance.

enforce: platform-level defaults in factory_reset_all or platform_settings_all
entity-level overrides in entity_setting_all (overrides platform defaults)
sub-entity-level overrides in sub_entity_setting_all (overrides entity settings)
each tier can independently override the tier above
rules.reason: Multi-tenant SaaS needs global defaults with per-client and per-location overrides. Three tiers covers virtually all cases.

trigger_when: any entity that goes through an in-flight phase before becoming permanent
enforce: in-flight records stored in _temp_ table during creation process
approved/completed records promoted to _header_all table
failed/rejected records moved to _failed_all or _rejected_all table
rules.reason: Keeps production entity tables clean. Temp table can be purged. Failed table provides analytics on drop-off.

trigger_when: multiple document or ID types for one entity (Aadhar, PAN, DL, Passport)
verification hub with multiple verification type spokes
enforce: hub table has linked_table column (varchar storing spoke table name)
hub tracks status, timestamps, and which spoke holds the data
each document/ID type gets its own spoke table with full structure
hub + spoke enables adding new document types without hub schema change
rules.reason: Different ID types have completely different fields. Forcing them into one table creates massive sparse nulls.

trigger_when: data correction workflows where original must be preserved
any system where human correction of system-generated data is needed
enforce: edited_* table mirrors primary table structure exactly
original data preserved in primary table
corrections stored in edited_* table with same primary key reference
rules.reason: Preserves audit trail of both what the system captured and what the human corrected it to.

trigger_when: one identity (mobile number, email) appears across multiple business entities
need to see all interactions for a person regardless of which entity they interacted with
enforce: line_no=0 master row for the identity (mobile, name, email)
line_no 1+ rows for each entity interaction (visit, transaction, application)
single lookup by identity gives complete cross-entity history
rules.reason: A mobile number can belong to a visitor, a guard, and an employee. Identity ledger unifies them without merging entity tables.

trigger_when: multiple third-party API providers for same service
enforce: priority column on service_provider_api table (lower = try first)
failed_cycle counter: increments every N consecutive failures
alert triggered when failed_cycle reaches multiple of threshold
last_failed_on and last_successed_on datetime columns
rules.reason: API providers go down. Schema-level failover logic ensures the application automatically routes to next provider.

trigger_when: any financial transaction that can fail
OTP or API call that has a failed outcome
enforce: failed transactions stored in dedicated _failed_all table
successful transactions in main _transaction_all table
never mix failed and successful records in same table
rules.reason: Failed transaction analysis requires different querying and retention than successful ones. Separation keeps main tables clean.

trigger_when: any async communication that needs guaranteed delivery
enforce: communication table acts as queue AND delivery log AND audit trail simultaneously
retry_count and max_retry columns for automatic retry logic
next_retry_at datetime for scheduled retry
status column: pending → processing → sent → delivered → failed
rules.reason: A DB queue never loses messages on server restart. Every message has a full delivery audit trail.

trigger_when: any system where mismatched data must be reviewed by a human
enforce: ambiguity_header_all table with its own full lifecycle (pending/approved/denied)
ambiguity_percentage column to quantify mismatch severity
ambiguity_found column to specify which fields mismatched
linked to alert, refund, and resolution workflows
rules.reason: Ambiguity is not just an error state — it is a business event requiring human review, refund eligibility, and audit trail.

trigger_when: any data that is accessed by month
enforce: month_year key column in format MM-YYYY or YYYY-MM
one column per day: day_1 through day_31 (or 1_day through 31_day)
line_no=0 for summary/master row; line_no 1+ for detail rows
NULL for days that don't exist in shorter months
rules.reason: Monthly calendar tables give O(1) access to any day's data. No date-range queries, no partitioning complexity.

trigger_when: choosing between ENUM, int, or varchar for status columns
enforce: ENUM: use for 2-5 immutable values that will never expand (Active/Inactive)
int + COMMENT: use for 5+ states, or states that may expand, or where ordering matters
varchar + COMMENT: use when values are codes humans need to read (Y/N, SO/CF/N)
rules.reason: Each encoding type has trade-offs. The selection must be intentional, not accidental.

enforce: store data_N (raw value) and diff_N (change from previous) columns side-by-side
compute diffs at INSERT time using previous row value
never compute diffs at read time on production tables
rules.reason: Read-time diff computation on large analytics tables is slow. Stored diffs make dashboard queries instant.

enforce: named columns (monday, tuesday, wednesday...) for day-of-week recurring weekly data
numbered columns (day_1, day_2... day_31) for date-of-month positional data
rules.reason: Named columns self-document weekly patterns. Numbered columns map directly to calendar date. Mixing them creates confusion.

trigger_when: configuration that changes infrequently but must have history
settings that have effective date ranges
enforce: from_date and to_date columns on every config record
new record inserted for each change; old record's to_date is closed
WHERE NOW() BETWEEN from_date AND to_date gives current active config
rules.reason: Point-in-time queries on configuration are essential for accurate historical transaction recreation.

trigger_when: building reusable features across multiple products
schema component that will be used in 2+ different databases
enforce: group 3-5 related tables into a self-contained module
module should function independently when dropped into any schema
document module dependencies clearly
rules.reason: Portable modules reduce development time for new products that share features (e.g. wallet module reused across 5 apps).

trigger_when: transactional tables used for period-based reporting
any table queried frequently by month/year
enforce: month_year column on every transaction row, set at INSERT time
format: MM-YYYY (e.g. '03-2025')
enables instant period filtering: WHERE month_year = '03-2025'
avoid: extracting month/year from datetime column at query time on large tables
rules.reason: Pre-tagged month_year avoids function-based filtering that prevents index use. Makes monthly reporting instant.

enforce: reporting_to column (FK) for upward traversal — who does this person report to
jr_emp_ids column (CSV of IDs) for downward traversal — who reports to this person
both on same entity row for O(1) hierarchy access in either direction
rules.reason: Self-referencing hierarchy with adjacency only requires recursive CTE for downward traversal. CSV shortcut avoids it.

trigger_when: any column that may not always have a value
conditional columns that depend on business rules
enforce: optional fields must be DEFAULT NULL
absence of value = NULL, not empty string
never use NOT NULL with DEFAULT '' for truly optional fields
avoid: NOT NULL DEFAULT '' — makes it impossible to distinguish 'not provided' from 'provided as empty'
using 0 or '0' as sentinel for absence of value
rules.reason: NULL semantics carry meaning. Empty string means 'provided but empty'. NULL means 'not provided'. They are not the same.

trigger_when: hierarchical data (org charts, category trees, location hierarchies)
tree-structured data of unknown or variable depth
enforce: variable-depth hierarchy: self-referencing adjacency list with parent_id FK
fixed-depth hierarchy (e.g. always 3 levels): inline level columns (level1_id, level2_id, level3_id)
rules.reason: Variable depth requires adjacency list. Fixed depth with inline columns avoids recursive queries entirely.

rules.rule_name: Circular FKs Acceptable for Bidirectional Relations
trigger_when: two tables that legitimately reference each other
enforce: circular FK constraints are acceptable when the business relationship is genuinely bidirectional
document circular dependency clearly in schema comments
avoid: forcing artificial hierarchy to avoid circular references when the business domain is circular
rules.reason: Some business relationships are genuinely bidirectional. Forcing them into a hierarchy creates false modelling.

trigger_when: domain-specific spatial data (road engineering, biometrics, GIS)
data with an established domain measurement system
enforce: use domain's native coordinate system as primary (chainage for roads, alpha/beta/gamma for biometrics)
GPS coordinates as supplementary when domain has its own native system
rules.reason: Domain experts use domain coordinates. GPS-only schema forces constant conversion that introduces errors.

rules.rule_name: Parallel Phase Statuses on Parent Entity
trigger_when: multi-phase processes where each phase is independent
competition rounds, project phases, registration stages
enforce: reg_phase_1, reg_phase_2, reg_phase_3 as independent tinyint columns on parent row
each phase is a separate boolean: cleared (1) or not cleared (0)
phases do not automatically cascade — each is independently set
rules.reason: Phases are not sequential status — a participant can clear phase 1 and fail phase 2 and later pass phase 3 independently.

trigger_when: records that become immutable after a specific event (approval, payment)
locked records where editing is prohibited
enforce: is_locked or lock_upload column (tinyint) on the entity
COMMENT explains lock condition: '1=locked after payment confirmed'
application checks flag before allowing any UPDATE
rules.reason: Immutability intent expressed in schema prevents future developers from accidentally allowing edits.

enforce: from_km/to_km or from_latitude/to_latitude columns on permission records
access control inherently tied to geographic range
spatial scope is part of the permission record, not a separate geo table
rules.reason: Geographic access control for linear infrastructure (roads, pipelines) is range-based, not point-based.

trigger_when: business ID columns that must be globally unique
enforce: ADD UNIQUE KEY on business ID columns (employee_id, invoice_no, order_id)
enforced at DB level via UNIQUE constraint, not only application layer
rules.reason: Application-layer uniqueness checks have a race condition window. DB-level UNIQUE constraint is atomic.

trigger_when: workflow tables with sequential status columns
tables documenting a process with a defined order
enforce: arrange columns left-to-right in temporal order of the workflow
requested_on → approved_on → permitted_on → completed_on
rules.reason: Column order in DDL narrates the workflow. A developer reading the CREATE TABLE immediately understands the process flow.

rules.rule_name: Granular Integer Status for Complex Domain State Machines
trigger_when: complex domain workflows with many states
enforce: use 5-15 granular integer states for complex domain state machines
document every state value in column COMMENT
do not collapse multiple distinct states into fewer coarse states
rules.reason: Coarse status loses operational nuance. Granular states enable precise querying and reporting at each stage.

trigger_when: any file URL that needs type context
enforce: file URL and file type always in same table, same row
paired columns: file1 + file_type1, file2 + file_type2
never store file URL in one table and file type in another
rules.reason: A file URL without type context is useless for rendering. Co-location ensures atomic retrieval of both.

trigger_when: multiple different entity types all requiring approval
approval logic needs to be centralised
enforce: single approval table with reference_id (FK value) + reference_table (table name as varchar)
handles all approval types without entity-specific approval tables
one approval table serves all entities in the system
rules.reason: Entity-specific approval tables create N duplicate approval schemas. One generic engine handles all.

trigger_when: calendar systems with both availability and notes per slot
enforce: a_N columns (tinyint) for availability flag per slot (0=unavailable, 1=available)
m_N columns (text) for content/notes per slot
paired: a_1 + m_1, a_2 + m_2... for each slot
rules.reason: Availability (boolean) and content (text) are different data types serving different query purposes. Pairing keeps them atomic.

enforce: N proposed slot columns on the row
agreed_slot column for the confirmed slot
per-party confirmation flags (party1_confirmed, party2_confirmed)
rules.reason: Multi-party scheduling state fits in a single row. Separate scheduling tables add unnecessary JOIN complexity.

enforce: reminder_count, last_reminder_on, next_reminder_on columns on entity row
breach_flag tinyint column set when deadline passed
deadline itself as a typed date column
rules.reason: Regulatory deadline state is always about the entity. Inline columns eliminate a JOIN to retrieve deadline status.

rules.rule_name: Deferred Entities with Expiry and Priority
trigger_when: demand that cannot be immediately fulfilled
requirement flags waiting for supply match
enforce: dedicated deferred/pending table
matched_id pointer column (0 or NULL until matched)
expiry_on datetime column
priority_flag column for queue ordering
rules.reason: Deferred entities have their own lifecycle (open → matched → expired). They are first-class entities, not afterthoughts.

rules.rule_name: Targets and Actuals in Separate Tables
enforce: target/budget table separate from actual/transaction table
never store planned and actual amounts in same row
rules.reason: Targets and actuals change for different reasons, at different frequencies, by different people. Separation prevents conflation.

trigger_when: forms that can be revised and resubmitted
enforce: update_count or resubmission_count integer column defaulting to 0
increment on every resubmission or correction
enables detection of habitual resubmitters
rules.reason: Resubmission count enables business intelligence (how many tries did it take?) and fraud detection (excessive corrections).

rules.rule_name: Product-Prefixed Columns in Singleton Policy Tables
trigger_when: singleton policy tables covering multiple products
enforce: prefix policy columns with product code (il_ for insurance loan, ccl_ for credit card loan)
single table can hold policies for multiple products via prefixed column groups
rules.reason: Product-prefixed columns in a singleton eliminate the need for one policy table per product.

rules.rule_name: Security and Fraud Tracking in Schema
enforce: dedicated blacklist/blocklist table with reason, blocked_by, blocked_on columns
fraud flags stored in schema — not only in application logs or external systems
rules.reason: Application logs are ephemeral. Schema-level fraud records are persistent, queryable, and part of the audit trail.

trigger_when: future modules planned but not yet built
architectural reservation for known upcoming features
enforce: create table with only PK column to reserve the name and signal intent
add COMMENT on table explaining what this will become
rules.reason: Schema design is communication. A placeholder table communicates to future developers: this space is intentionally reserved.

rules.rule_name: Flat Tables for Fixed Third-Party API Responses
trigger_when: storing responses from third-party APIs with fixed known structure
government API responses (Aadhar, PAN, DL verification)
enforce: flatten fixed-structure API response into typed columns
one column per field in the API response
do not store as JSON blob when response structure is stable
avoid: JSON blob storage for fixed-schema API responses — makes field querying impossible
rules.reason: Fixed-structure API responses deserve typed columns for queryability, validation, and index support.

trigger_when: small fixed set of role combinations
user types that are a product of two roles
enforce: use composite integer for small fixed role combinations (1=owner, 2=employee, 3=both)
document all values in COMMENT
rules.reason: For 3-5 fixed combinations, a composite integer is simpler than a join table.

rules.rule_name: Operational State on Reusable Entity Row
trigger_when: reusable physical or virtual assets (parking slots, devices, watches)
assets that cycle through available/allocated/suspended states
enforce: current operational state tracked directly on entity row (available/allocated/suspended)
entry_exit_status and operational_status as separate typed columns on the asset row
rules.reason: Asset state must be readable in O(1) without joining to allocation tables. The asset row is the source of truth for its own state.

trigger_when: any business algorithm with configurable inputs
enforce: min_count, max_count, ratios, intervals stored as typed schema columns
changing business rules = data UPDATE, not code deployment
parameters are versioned with from_date/to_date
rules.reason: Algorithm parameters in code require redeployment to change. Parameters in schema can be updated by operations team.

trigger_when: mostly-stable configuration with occasional dynamic extensions
settings where some keys are known and some are dynamic
enforce: typed columns for known stable configuration fields
name/value pair rows (or JSON column) for dynamic/extensible configuration
both mechanisms on same configuration table
rules.reason: Typed columns give performance and validation for known fields. Name-value pairs give flexibility for unknown future fields.

rules.rule_name: Fixed-Depth Category Hierarchy with Separate Level Tables
trigger_when: fixed-depth hierarchies where each level has its own independent attributes
enforce: separate table per level: category_header_all, sub_category_header_all, item_header_all
each level table has its own attributes independent of other levels
rules.reason: Fixed-depth hierarchies with independent attributes per level cannot be cleanly represented in a single self-referencing table.

trigger_when: approval workflows with in-flight, approved, and rejected states
any workflow with three distinct terminal states
enforce: _temp_ table: in-flight records being processed
_header_all table: approved and permanently active records
_failed_all or _rejected_all table: rejected, failed, or cancelled records
data promotes between tables as state advances — never updates in place
rules.reason: State promotion via table movement keeps each table clean and purpose-specific. Query performance is better as tables stay small.

rules.rule_name: UUID Only for Genuinely Cross-System Entities
trigger_when: entities that must be globally unique across multiple independent systems
IDs that will be shared between databases that cannot coordinate
enforce: use UUID as PK only when global uniqueness across independently-operating systems is required
use auto-increment int for all internal entities
avoid: UUID as default PK choice for internal entities
UUID where auto-increment int is sufficient — UUID adds index overhead
rules.reason: UUID PKs have higher storage cost, worse index performance, and worse INSERT performance. Use only when genuinely needed.

trigger_when: CSV accumulator columns with fixed slot limits
numbered column sets with capacity ceilings
enforce: table_performance_information_all tracks fill level of CSV and numbered columns
alert threshold column: notify when column approaches capacity
stop flag column: halt writes when column is full
rules.reason: CSV columns and numbered slot columns have hard capacity limits. Breaching them silently corrupts data.

trigger_when: any system where UI access is controlled per role
enforce: every screen, form, and action registered as rows in a process registry table
access control references form_ids and process_ids from registry
adding a new screen = inserting a row, not writing code
rules.reason: Code-based access control requires deployment for every permission change. DB-based control is instant and auditable.

rules.rule_name: Error Logging as Schema Entity with Lifecycle
trigger_when: any operational error that requires follow-up action
enforce: error log table with status lifecycle: open → acknowledged → resolved
error_datetime, type, service_provider, error_message, loss_amount columns
errors are first-class entities — not just log files
rules.reason: Errors with financial or operational impact need assignment, tracking, and resolution confirmation — not just a log entry.

trigger_when: high-volume transaction tables needing periodic consolidation
tables that grow too large for direct reporting queries
enforce: Individual transactions → daily consolidation table → monthly consolidation table
consolidated_on timestamp marks when each consolidation ran
historical individual records preserved; consolidation is additive
rules.reason: Running SUM/COUNT on years of individual transactions is slow. Tiered consolidation makes period reporting instant.

rules.rule_name: JSON Strings in Numbered Slot Columns
trigger_when: numbered slot columns where each slot needs multiple related attributes
exam question slots with answer, status, and time
notification slots with ID, body, and delivery status
enforce: encode as compact JSON string within varchar column when slot needs multiple attributes
use when: slot count is fixed, data is read-mostly, multi-attribute always retrieved as unit
example: question_1 = '{"que_id":101,"marked_ans":"B","status":1,"correct_ans":"B"}'
avoid: separate columns for each sub-attribute of a numbered slot when attributes are always retrieved together
rules.reason: When a slot's sub-attributes are always retrieved together and never individually queried, JSON encoding keeps the schema compact.

rules.rule_name: JSON CHECK Constraints on Calendar Columns
trigger_when: monthly calendar columns storing structured JSON objects per day
numbered day columns with multi-attribute JSON content
enforce: add CHECK (json_valid(day_N)) on numbered calendar columns storing JSON
enforces JSON format at DB level — not only application layer
rules.reason: JSON validity enforced at DB level prevents malformed JSON from being stored, which would break all reads of that slot.

rules.rule_name: Dual-Layer Index + Detail in Numbered Slot Columns
trigger_when: numbered slot columns where slots contain complex objects
blacklist tables with mobile numbers and visitor details
batch record tables where individual item lookup is needed
enforce: parallel key columns (mobile_1...mobile_N) for fast indexed lookup — searchable without parsing
parallel detail columns (detail_1...detail_N) for full record retrieval
key columns enable WHERE mobile_N = '9876543210' without touching detail columns
rules.reason: Without key columns, finding whether a specific value exists requires parsing all detail JSON/CSV slots. O(N) vs O(1).

trigger_when: Laravel, Django, Rails, or any framework generates its own tables in the same database
framework migration system manages schema alongside custom tables
enforce: leave framework-generated tables as-is (migrations, jobs, sessions, cache, cache_locks, failed_jobs)
never rename or restructure framework tables into your naming convention
framework tables are infrastructure — managed by framework, not by your schema conventions
avoid: renaming 'jobs' to 'job_header_all'
renaming 'sessions' to 'session_header_all'
any modification of framework-owned tables
rules.reason: Framework updates regenerate or reference these tables by their exact original names. Renaming them breaks the framework.

rules.rule_name: Relationship-Scoped Permissions Inline on Linkage Row
trigger_when: network relationships between entities where access scope varies per relationship
broker-to-broker connections with filtered property access
agency-to-campus linkages with specific authority levels
enforce: encode permission scope directly on the linkage/relationship row
allowed categories, types, areas, access_type stored on the relationship record itself
the linkage row IS the access control record — no separate permission table
avoid: separate permission table for relationship-specific access control
rules.reason: Relationship permissions are intrinsic to the relationship. Separating them requires an extra JOIN and creates synchronisation risk.

rules.rule_name: old_ Prefix for Superseded Schema-Version Tables
trigger_when: schema redesign retaining historical data from prior version
tables replaced by new design but kept for legacy data access
enforce: old_ prefix for tables superseded by a schema redesign but retained for history
old_ tables are read-only relics — never written to after cutover
document in table COMMENT: when superseded and what replaced it
avoid: using old_ prefix for ongoing operational archives — use _archive_all for that
confusing old_ (schema version relic) with _archive_all (ongoing operational history)
rules.reason: old_ signals 'this existed in a prior schema design'. _archive_all signals 'this is an ongoing copy of live data'. They are different things.
